::: {.solutions}

Logarithms turn a hard equation (an unknown in the exponent, a product, a ratio) into an easy one — **as long
as you obey the laws and watch the domain**. TMUA/MAT and their cousins (STEP, PAT, admissions mocks) rarely
ask you to "evaluate a log"; they ask you to **rewrite** with the laws, **substitute** to expose a hidden
quadratic, **solve** and reject the impossible root, handle a **base-flip** inequality, or decide **how many**
solutions exist as a parameter moves. This clinic drills every one of those, hardest cases included.

::: {.fs-card}
### 1 · The domain trap
$\log_a(\text{something})$ needs that something $>0$. Every root you find must be checked
against **all** the log arguments — a value that makes any argument $\le0$ is **rejected** (extraneous).
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 2 · The base-size trap
$y=\log_a x$ **increases** if $a>1$ but **decreases** if $0<a<1$ — so when you take
logs (or drop them) across an inequality with $0<a<1$, the inequality **flips**.
:::

::::

:::::

**On this page:** 1. Laws & change of base · 2. Solving equations (domain & extraneous) · 3. Exponential /
substitution equations · 4. Inequalities · 5. Counting solutions with a parameter · 6. Log graphs

## 1 · Laws & change of base

### Question 1

::: {.question}
Given that $\log_2 5=a$, write **(i)** $\log_2 40$ and **(ii)** $\log_2 0.16$ in terms of $a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(express one log in terms of another)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — break the argument into prime factors, then apply product/quotient/power
:::

**Answer: (i) $3+a$; (ii) $2-2a$.**

- **(i)** $40=2^{3}\times5$, so $\log_2 40=3+\log_2 5=3+a$.
- **(ii)** $0.16=\dfrac{16}{100}=\dfrac{2^{2}}{5^{2}}$, so $\log_2 0.16=2-2\log_2 5=2-2a$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 2

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_2 x+\log_4 x+\log_{16}x=\dfrac74\;$ for $x>0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a tower of bases — change of base first)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — write $\log_4,\log_{16}$ in base $2$; the coefficients form a neat sum
:::

**Answer: $x=2$.**

Put everything in base $2$: $\log_4 x=\tfrac12\log_2 x$ and $\log_{16}x=\tfrac14\log_2 x$. So
$$\Big(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14\Big)\log_2 x=\tfrac74\log_2 x=\tfrac74\ \Rightarrow\ \log_2 x=1\ \Rightarrow\ x=2.$$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 3

::: {.question}
Given $\;\log_2 x+\log_2 y=5\;$ and $\;\log_2\!\dfrac{x}{y}=1$, find $x$ and $y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a simultaneous pair)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — treat $\log_2 x$ and $\log_2 y$ as the unknowns of a linear system
:::

**Answer: $x=8,\ y=4$.**

Let $X=\log_2 x,\ Y=\log_2 y$. The laws give $X+Y=5$ and $X-Y=1$, so $X=3,\ Y=2$. Hence $x=2^{3}=8$ and
$y=2^{2}=4$. *(Check: $xy=32=2^{5}$ ✓, $x/y=2$ ✓.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## 2 · Solving equations (domain & extraneous roots)

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — solve a log equation in four moves

1. **Collect** every log onto one side with the laws until you have $\log_a(\text{expr})=\text{number}$ (or
   $\log_a P=\log_a Q$).
2. **Undo** the log: $\log_a P=\log_a Q\Rightarrow P=Q$; $\log_a P=c\Rightarrow P=a^{c}$.
3. **Solve** the resulting (often quadratic) equation.
4. **Check the domain** — throw away any root that makes an original log's argument $\le0$.
:::

### Question 4

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_{10}x+\log_{10}(x-3)=1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a root must be rejected)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — combine to one log, undo, then test each root in the original domain
:::

**Answer: $x=5$ only.**

$$\log_{10}\big(x(x-3)\big)=1\ \Rightarrow\ x(x-3)=10\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}-3x-10=0\ \Rightarrow\ (x-5)(x+2)=0.$$
The original needs $x>0$ **and** $x-3>0$, i.e. $x>3$. So $x=-2$ is **rejected** and only $x=5$ survives.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 5

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_2 x+\log_2(x+2)=3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(same trap, base 2)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — one log per side isn't required; combine first, then reject
:::

**Answer: $x=2$ only.**

$\log_2\big(x(x+2)\big)=3\Rightarrow x(x+2)=8\Rightarrow x^{2}+2x-8=0\Rightarrow(x+4)(x-2)=0$. The domain needs
$x>0$, so $x=-4$ is **rejected**; $x=2$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

---

### Question 6

::: {.question}
Solve $\;(\log_2 x)^{2}-\log_2\!\big(x^{2}\big)=3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a hidden quadratic in $\log x$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — substitute $u=\log_2 x$; $\log_2(x^{2})=2u$, not $u^{2}$
:::

**Answer: $x=8$ or $x=\tfrac12$.**

Beware $\log_2(x^{2})=2\log_2 x$ (power law), **not** $(\log_2 x)^{2}$. Let $u=\log_2 x$:
$$u^{2}-2u-3=0\Rightarrow(u-3)(u+1)=0\Rightarrow u=3\text{ or }-1,$$
so $x=8$ or $x=\tfrac12$. Both positive — **both valid**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

---

### Question 7

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_3 x+\log_x 3=\dfrac52\;$ for $x>0,\ x\ne1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a log and its reciprocal)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log_x 3=\dfrac1{\log_3 x}$; substitute $u=\log_3 x$ to get $u+\tfrac1u$
:::

**Answer: $x=9$ or $x=\sqrt3$.**

By change of base $\log_x 3=\dfrac1{\log_3 x}$. Let $u=\log_3 x$:
$$u+\frac1u=\frac52\ \Rightarrow\ 2u^{2}-5u+2=0\ \Rightarrow\ (2u-1)(u-2)=0\ \Rightarrow\ u=\tfrac12\text{ or }2.$$
So $\log_3 x=\tfrac12\Rightarrow x=\sqrt3$, or $\log_3 x=2\Rightarrow x=9$. Both are in the domain.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## 3 · Exponential / substitution equations

::: {.callout-tip}
## Concept — when the unknown is in the exponent, substitute the power

An equation like $2^{2x}-5\cdot2^{x}+4=0$ is a **quadratic in $t=2^{x}$**. Solve for $t$, then take logs to
recover $x$ — but only for $t>0$ (a power is always positive, so a **negative or zero $t$ is rejected**).
:::

### Question 8

::: {.question}
Solve $\;2^{2x}-5\cdot2^{x}+4=0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a quadratic in $2^{x}$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $t=2^{x}>0$; solve the quadratic, keep positive $t$, then log
:::

**Answer: $x=0$ or $x=2$.**

Let $t=2^{x}$ (so $2^{2x}=t^{2}$): $t^{2}-5t+4=0\Rightarrow(t-1)(t-4)=0\Rightarrow t=1$ or $4$. Both positive,
so $2^{x}=1\Rightarrow x=0$, and $2^{x}=4\Rightarrow x=2$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 9

::: {.question}
How many real solutions does $\;(\log_{10}x)^{2}=\log_{10}\!\big(x^{2}\big)$ have, and what are they?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(count the roots of a log equation)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log(x^{2})=2\log x$ only for $x>0$; factor and count
:::

**Answer: two — $x=1$ and $x=100$.**

The domain is $x>0$, where $\log_{10}(x^{2})=2\log_{10}x$. With $u=\log_{10}x$:
$$u^{2}=2u\Rightarrow u(u-2)=0\Rightarrow u=0\text{ or }2,$$
so $x=10^{0}=1$ or $x=10^{2}=100$. Two solutions. *(The trap: cancelling a "$\log x$" would lose the root
$x=1$.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## 4 · Inequalities

### Question 10

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_{1/2}x>3$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a base between 0 and 1 flips the sign)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $0<a<1$: $\log_a$ is **decreasing**, so undoing the log reverses the inequality
:::

**Answer: $\left(0,\tfrac18\right)$.**

Base $\tfrac12<1$, so $\log_{1/2}$ is **decreasing** and removing it **reverses** the sign:
$x<\left(\tfrac12\right)^{3}=\tfrac18$. With the domain $x>0$: $0<x<\tfrac18$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

---

### Question 11

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_2(x-1)<3$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the domain supplies a boundary)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — an increasing-base inequality, but the argument must stay positive
:::

**Answer: $(1,9)$.**

Base $2>1$ keeps the sign: $x-1<2^{3}=8\Rightarrow x<9$. The log needs $x-1>0\Rightarrow x>1$. So $1<x<9$ —
the lower end comes from the **domain**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 12

::: {.question}
Solve $\;(\log_2 x)^{2}-3\log_2 x+2\le0$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a quadratic inequality in $\log x$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — substitute $u=\log_2 x$, solve the quadratic inequality, convert back
:::

**Answer: $[2,4]$.**

With $u=\log_2 x$: $u^{2}-3u+2\le0\Rightarrow(u-1)(u-2)\le0\Rightarrow1\le u\le2$. Since $\log_2$ is
increasing, $1\le\log_2 x\le2\Rightarrow2\le x\le4$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## 5 · Counting solutions with a parameter

::: {.callout-tip}
## Concept — reduce to a simpler equation, then read the count off the parameters

Rewrite the log equation with the laws until it is a **linear or quadratic** equation (or a line-meets-curve
picture). The number of **valid** solutions is then decided by a **sign** or a **discriminant** in the
parameters — always finishing with the domain check ($x>0$, arguments $>0$).
:::

### Question 13

::: {.question}
The number of **positive** solutions $x$ to $\;\log_2 x=\log_2(x+a)+b\;$ (with $a,b$ non-zero real) is
&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** zero if $ab<1$, or one if $ab>1$ &nbsp; **B** one if $ab<1$, or two if $ab>1$ &nbsp;
**C** one if $ab<0$, or zero if $ab>0$ &nbsp; **D** zero if $ab<0$, or one if $ab>0$ &nbsp; **E** one if
$ab<1$, or zero if $ab>1$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the parameter classic)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — quotient law $\to$ a linear equation; the sign of $ab$ decides the count
:::

**Answer: C (one if $ab<0$, zero if $ab>0$).**

**Collect the logs:** $\log_2\dfrac{x}{x+a}=b\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{x+a}=2^{b}=:k$ ($k>0,\ k\ne1$). Solving,
$x=\dfrac{ka}{1-k}$; note $x+a=\dfrac{x}{k}>0$ automatically once $x>0$, so the **only** constraint is $x>0$.

- $b>0\Rightarrow k>1\Rightarrow1-k<0$: need $ka<0$, i.e. $a<0$.
- $b<0\Rightarrow0<k<1\Rightarrow1-k>0$: need $ka>0$, i.e. $a>0$.

Both say $a,b$ have **opposite signs** ($ab<0$) $\to$ **one** solution; $ab>0\to$ **none**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 14

::: {.question}
For $c>0$, how many positive solutions does $\;\ln x=cx\;$ have, and at which $c$ does the count change?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a line meets the log curve)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — solutions of $\ln x=cx$ are crossings of $y=\ln x$ and $y=cx$; the tangent value of $c$ is the border
:::

**Answer: two for $0<c<\tfrac1e$, one (tangent) at $c=\tfrac1e$, none for $c>\tfrac1e$.**

Solutions are crossings of the line $y=cx$ with $y=\ln x$. The border is **tangency**: at $x=t$ we need
$\ln t=ct$ and $\dfrac1t=c$. Then $ct=1$, so $\ln t=1\Rightarrow t=e,\ c=\dfrac1e$. Hence $c=\tfrac1e$ gives
one solution ($x=e$), $0<c<\tfrac1e$ two, and $c>\tfrac1e$ none.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(0.05,12,600)
plt.figure(figsize=(5.2,3.2)); plt.plot(x,np.log(x),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y=ln x')
for c,col,ls,lab in [(1/np.e,'crimson','-','y=x/e (tangent, c=1/e)'),(0.15,'0.6','--','c<1/e: two'),(0.5,'green','--','c>1/e: none')]:
    plt.plot(x,c*x,color=col,ls=ls,lw=1.3,label=lab)
plt.plot(np.e,1,'ko',ms=4); plt.ylim(-2,3); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.5); plt.legend(fontsize=7.5)
plt.title('ln x = cx: tangent at x=e, c=1/e',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## 6 · Log graphs

::: {.callout-tip}
## Concept — read a log graph off its asymptote and one point

$y=\log_a x$ ($a>1$) passes through $(1,0)$ and $(a,1)$, climbs slowly, and has the $y$-axis as a **vertical
asymptote** ($y\to-\infty$). Transformations move it: $y=\log_a(x-p)+q$ shifts the asymptote to $x=p$ and the
curve up by $q$. Always state the **domain** — the argument must stay positive.
:::

### Question 15

::: {.question}
Sketch $y=\log_2(x-2)+1$: state its domain, its vertical asymptote, and where it crosses the line $y=1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a shifted log)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $y=\log_2(x-2)+1$: domain, asymptote, two easy points
:::

**Answer: domain $x>2$; asymptote $x=2$; crosses $y=1$ at $x=3$ (and passes through $(4,2)$).**

Argument $x-2>0\Rightarrow$ domain $x>2$, asymptote $x=2$. Then $\log_2(x-2)=0$ at $x=3$ ($y=1$) and
$\log_2(x-2)=1$ at $x=4$ ($y=2$). It is the standard $\log_2$ curve slid $2$ right and $1$ up.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(2.02,10,500)
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0)); plt.plot(x,np.log2(x-2)+1,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.axvline(2,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1); plt.plot(3,1,'o',color='crimson'); plt.plot(4,2,'o',color='crimson')
plt.annotate('(3,1)',(3,1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,-10),fontsize=8)
plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.5); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.ylim(-3,5)
plt.title('y = log₂(x−2)+1: asymptote x=2, through (3,1),(4,2)',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}

### Question 16

::: {.question}
Contrast the graphs of $y=\ln\!\big(x^{2}\big)$ and $y=2\ln x$. Are they the same curve? Give the domain and
symmetry of each.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*($\ln x^{2}$ is not $2\ln x$ — mind the domain)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\ln(x^{2})$ is even (both signs of $x$); $2\ln x$ lives only on $x>0$
:::

**Answer: they agree only for $x>0$. $\ln(x^{2})$ is defined for all $x\ne0$ and is **even**; $2\ln x$ is
defined only for $x>0$.**

The power law carries a modulus: $\ln(x^{2})=2\ln|x|$. For $x>0$ this is $2\ln x$; for $x<0$ the left side is
still defined ($x^{2}>0$) while $2\ln x$ is not. So $y=\ln(x^{2})$ is the even curve with a mirror branch on
$x<0$; $y=2\ln x$ is only its right half. Writing $\ln(x^{2})=2\ln x$ silently **drops the left branch**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
xn=np.linspace(-8,-0.03,400); xp=np.linspace(0.03,8,400)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(6.8,2.9))
ax[0].plot(xn,np.log(xn**2),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); ax[0].plot(xp,np.log(xp**2),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
ax[0].set_title('y = ln(x²): even, x≠0',fontsize=9)
ax[1].plot(xp,2*np.log(xp),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); ax[1].set_title('y = 2 ln x: only x>0',fontsize=9)
for a in ax: a.axvline(0,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1); a.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.5); a.grid(alpha=0.25); a.set_ylim(-4,5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Memorise — logarithms

- **Laws:** product $\to$ sum, quotient $\to$ difference, power $\to$ front coefficient; change of base
  $\log_a x=\dfrac{\log_b x}{\log_b a}=\dfrac1{\log_x a}$.
- **Solve:** collect to one log $\to$ undo $\to$ solve $\to$ **check every argument is $>0$** (reject
  extraneous roots).
- **Hidden quadratics:** $u=\log_a x$ turns $(\log x)^2$-equations into quadratics; $t=a^{x}>0$ turns
  exponential equations into quadratics (reject $t\le0$).
- **$\log_2(x^{2})=2\log_2 x$** only for $x>0$; in general it is $2\log_2\lvert x\rvert$.
- **Inequalities:** base $>1$ keeps the sign, base $0<a<1$ **flips** it; the argument $>0$ often supplies the
  other boundary.
- **Counting with a parameter:** rewrite to linear/quadratic (or line-meets-curve), then a **sign of $ab$** or
  a **tangent** value fixes the number of valid solutions.
- **Graphs:** $y=\log_a(x-p)+q$ — asymptote $x=p$, through $(p+1,q)$ and $(p+a,q+1)$; state the domain.
:::

:::
